one_line: Hands-on test of Meta's Muse Glimmer and NVIDIA's Nemotron Lightning 3.5 (both ~30B, local via Ollama) on three agentic tasks; Glimmer passes two of three, Lightning fails all three.
summary: The host compares two open-weight models released the same week, Meta's Muse Glimmer (a distilled Muse Spark) and NVIDIA's Nemotron Lightning 3.5 (a mixture-of-experts model), on an RTX 5090 workstation served through Ollama and driven by OpenCode. The first task asks each model to build a single web page explaining an ESP32-C3 wiring setup; Lightning produces a blank page with dead buttons even after a second correction round, while Glimmer produces a working but incomplete page. The second task has the models edit a Premiere project via a custom UXP plugin and an Epidemic Sound MCP server to build an "AI" montage with music; Lightning fast-calls tools but damages the timeline, while Glimmer completes the edit correctly and handles a follow-up request. The third task asks for percentages from NVIDIA's FY2026 10-K; Lightning's SEC fetch fails, it falls back to search, and reports wrong numbers (23% vs the filing's 22% and 14%), while Glimmer recovers the correct 36% combined figure despite some failed fetches. The host scores Glimmer 2/3 and says he would consider using it day to day; the sample is one run per model per task, and the title and verdict are more emphatic than the evidence supports.

key_ideas.idea: Both models are pitched as ~30B and consumer-friendly, but they are built differently: Glimmer is a dense distillation, Lightning is a mixture-of-experts model.
key_ideas.detail: Glimmer is a distilled version of Muse Spark, with quantized builds for M4/M5 Macs. Lightning routes each token to a few expert subnetworks, so the host says only a fraction of the parameters are active per token. The transcript gives both 30B and 13B total for Lightning, so the total size is unclear.

key_ideas.idea: Glimmer ships with D-Flash speculative decoding, where a small drafter proposes a block of tokens and the main model verifies it.
key_ideas.detail: The host claims roughly a 3x speed-up without quality loss, but the video does not measure throughput; the claim is untested here.

key_ideas.idea: On paper the two differ mainly in vision and context: Glimmer sees images and has about 128K context, Lightning has no vision and about 1M context.
key_ideas.detail: Both support tool calling. The host expects Lightning to suit large-document work and Glimmer short dense back-and-forths, which the later tests partly contradict.

key_ideas.idea: Lightning failed the single-file web page task twice, while Glimmer produced a partially working page.
key_ideas.detail: Lightning gave a blank page with non-functional buttons after about 5 minutes, and the same after a second round of about 6 minutes. Glimmer took about 2m50s, produced working buttons, a pin layout and tooltips, but no real wiring diagram.

key_ideas.idea: In the Premiere edit, Lightning's fast tool calls were not enough. It put music on the speaker track, deleted speaker audio while trying to fix it, and damaged the timeline.
key_ideas.detail: Glimmer was slower but correct: it put the music on a separate track, trimmed it to the video length, added a fade-out, and swapped the track when asked. The host treats error recovery and state awareness as the discriminating skills.

key_ideas.idea: On the 10-K question, a failed fetch led Lightning to fall back to general search, and it reported wrong figures with confidence.
key_ideas.detail: Lightning answered 23% combined (about 13% and 10%, data center). The filing says 22% and 14%, 36% combined. Glimmer hit some failed fetches but recovered the correct figures in about 3 minutes.

key_ideas.idea: The host's verdict is 2 of 3 for Glimmer, and he questions NVIDIA's benchmarks given the Lightning results.
key_ideas.detail: This is one run per model per task on a single workstation, so the verdict is anecdotal. The skepticism about published benchmarks is an opinion, not something this test measured.

techniques.name: Same-prompt, multi-round correction test
techniques.how: Send an identical prompt to each model, then give up to two follow-up prompts that name the specific bug. Mark the task failed if the output is still broken after the last round. Record wall-clock time per round.
techniques.when: Comparing agentic coding or task models on fixed tasks where a human judges the result.

techniques.name: Serve two local models and drive them from an agent CLI
techniques.how: Load both models on an Ollama server and point OpenCode at it with a JSON config that lists the two models and the MCP servers. The video shows the config in a screen capture but does not show exact keys; a GitHub gist with the prompt is referenced.
techniques.when: Quick local A/B tests of open models for tool-using agent work on a single GPU box.

techniques.name: Expose a desktop editor to models through a custom UXP plugin
techniques.how: Build an Adobe Premiere plugin using UXP that connects through Adobe Bridge and exposes editor actions as tools. Any tool-calling model can then drive the NLE. The plugin repo link is in the video description and was not captured in the transcript.
techniques.when: When an agent needs to operate a GUI application through structured actions rather than screen control.

techniques.name: Check numbers against the source document
techniques.how: When a model extracts figures from a long filing, compare each figure with the primary source (here the 10-K) and check whether the reported 'cross-check' actually appears in the cited section.
techniques.when: Any document-QA or financial-extraction task, especially when the model had a failed tool call.

techniques.name: Treat tool-error fallback as a test case
techniques.how: Break a fetch on purpose or observe a failed one, and check whether the agent reports the failure or silently answers from a weaker source. Lightning's fallback to general search produced confident wrong numbers.
techniques.when: Evaluating agent reliability for research or retrieval tasks.

numbers.claim: Both models are described as 30B parameters.
D-Flash drafter proposes a block of 16 (transcript says 'words', likely tokens) per step, with a claimed 3x speed-up and no quality loss; not measured in the video.
Lightning is described as about 13B total parameters with about 3B active per token.
Context windows: Glimmer about 128K tokens, Lightning about 1M tokens.
Test rig: RTX 5090 with 64 GB DDR5.
Web page task: Lightning about 5 min (round 1) and about 6 min (round 2), both broken; Glimmer about 2m50s, partly working.
10-K task: Lightning reported about 23% combined (13% + 10%); the filing shows 22% + 14% = 36%. Glimmer took about 3 minutes and reported 22%, 14%, 36%.
Final score: Glimmer 2 of 3 tasks passed, Lightning 0 of 3.

hot_takes: Lightning is called 'probably the worst model I've ever tested' (title says 'DISASTER'), an emotional verdict based on one run per task.
The host questions whether NVIDIA tests its own model and whether its published benchmarks can be trusted, without evidence from this test.
The host says he would consider using Glimmer daily when Claude token usage runs out, but this is a personal preference rather than a measured result.

relevance.why: The video tests two 30B-class open models on a single RTX 5090 with tool calls, the same class of hardware and models InferCraft targets. The 10-K failure, where a failed fetch led to confident wrong numbers, is a concrete failure mode for the MemoryMesh and eval story.
relevance.action: Add a tool-failure case and a known-answer filing extraction (with a ground-truth figure) to the agent eval set, and run it against any new open model before routing traffic to it.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps the Claude Code CLI; the tool-error fallback behavior seen here is relevant to how a harness should surface failed tool calls rather than let the model answer silently.
relevance.action: When adding any non-Claude backend to ProsHarness, add a check that a failed tool call surfaces as a failure rather than a fallback answer.
